question.prompt: Nondegenerate \(\triangle ABC\) has integer side lengths, \(\overline{BD}\) is an angle bisector, \(AD = 3,\) and \(DC = 8.\) What is the smallest possible value of the perimeter?

solutions.explanation:
The angle bisector connects the given pieces of \(AC\) to the two unknown sides. Since \(AC=3+8=11\), the angle-bisector theorem gives
\[
\frac{AB}{BC}=\frac{AD}{DC}=\frac38.
\]
Because \(3:8\) is a ratio in lowest terms and both side lengths are integers, write \(AB=3k\) and \(BC=8k\), where \(k\) is a positive integer.

The triangle must be nondegenerate, so its side inequalities are strict. In particular,
\[
3k+8k>11
\quad\text{and}\quad
3k+11>8k.
\]
These give \(k>1\) and \(k<11/5\). The remaining inequality, \(8k+11>3k\), holds automatically for positive \(k\). Thus the only possible integer is \(k=2\).

The resulting sides are \(6,16,11\), which satisfy all three strict triangle inequalities. Their angle bisector divides the side of length \(11\) in the ratio \(6:16=3:8\), giving the required pieces \(3\) and \(8\). Therefore the smallest possible perimeter is
\[
6+16+11=\boxed{33},
\]
choice \(\text{B}\).
solutions.title: Use the angle-bisector ratio
